summary: Describes version 1.5 of the PKCS #1 standard from RSA Laboratories for encrypting data and creating signatures with the RSA public-key cryptosystem. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 2437.

plainLanguage.summary: A recipe for locking a message with a public key that anyone can use, so only the owner of the matching private key can open it.

questions: how does rsa encryption work in pkcs
what is block type in rsa encryption
subtitle: RSA public-key encryption and signatures, version 1.5

tldr.problem: Applications need a standard way to encrypt data and create digital signatures using RSA public-key cryptography.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #1 version 1.5 specifies how to format and encrypt data with RSA keys, how to create signatures with message digests (MD2, MD4, MD5), and defines the syntax for RSA public and private keys.
tldr.outcome: PKCS #1 v1.5 became widely used in digital certificates and secure communications. RFC 2437 superseded it with version 2.0 (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 for signatures, RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 for encryption), and weaknesses in v1.5 padding led to recommendations for newer schemes.

today: RFC 2437 (PKCS #1 v2.0) superseded this document in October 1998. RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 remains acceptable for digital signatures but requires careful implementation. For encryption, OAEP padding is now recommended due to vulnerabilities discovered in v1.5 encryption schemes.

sections.title: Overview and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2313 (PKCS #1 version 1.5) describes RSA encryption methods for two main uses. For digital signatures, the content is first reduced to a message digest (MD2, MD4, or MD5), then encrypted with the sender's private key. For digital envelopes, content is encrypted under a symmetric key (like DES), and that key is encrypted with the recipient's RSA public key.

The RFC also specifies syntax for RSA public and private keys, compatible with X.509 certificates and Privacy-Enhanced Mail (PEM). It defines three signature algorithms combining each message digest with RSA: MD2WithRSAEncryption, MD4WithRSAEncryption, and MD5WithRSAEncryption.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is the instruction manual for using RSA to lock messages and prove who sent them.

sections.title: Key Generation and Syntax
sections.content:
An entity generates an RSA key pair by choosing a public exponent e and two distinct large random primes p and q. The public modulus is n = pq. The private exponent d is chosen so that de - 1 is divisible by both p - 1 and q - 1.

The modulus n must be at least 12 octets (96 bits) long to accommodate the block formats in the RFC. For security, modern practice recommends at least 2048 bits.

The RFC specifies the ASN.1 syntax for RSAPublicKey (modulus and public exponent) and RSAPrivateKey (version, modulus, both exponents, both primes, and CRT coefficients for efficiency).
sections.plainLanguage: You pick two secret big prime numbers and do math to create a public lock and a secret key to open it.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption
sections.content:
The encryption process has four steps: block formatting (adds structure and padding), octet-string-to-integer conversion, RSA computation (raising to a power modulo n), and integer-to-octet-string conversion.

The block format is 00 || BT || PS || 00 || D, where BT is the block type (00, 01, or 02), PS is a padding string, and D is the data. The length of data D must not exceed k - 11 octets, where k is the modulus length, ensuring at least 8 octets of padding for security.

For public-key operations (encryption), block type 02 uses pseudorandom nonzero padding. For private-key operations (signing), block type 01 uses FF bytes for padding. This design prevents certain attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Before locking the message, you wrap it in padding to prevent attackers from guessing the contents.

sections.title: Digital Signatures
sections.content:
To create a signature, the message is first digested (MD2, MD4, or MD5), then the digest and algorithm identifier are encoded into an ASN.1 DigestInfo structure and BER-encoded. This becomes the data D in the encryption block (with block type 01), which is then encrypted with the private key to produce the signature.

To verify, the signature is decrypted with the public key, the DigestInfo is decoded, the message is digested with the identified algorithm, and the computed digest is compared to the received one. If they match, the signature is valid.

The RFC notes that including the algorithm identifier in DigestInfo limits damage if one hash algorithm is broken; an attacker who breaks MD2 cannot forge signatures on messages using MD5.
sections.plainLanguage: You turn a message into a fingerprint, lock that fingerprint with your secret key, and send it along with the message. Anyone can unlock it with your public key to prove you sent it.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The RFC discusses security considerations throughout. For block type 02 (public-key operations), pseudorandom padding must be generated independently for each encryption. The minimum padding length of eight octets prevents attackers from recovering data by trying all possible encryption blocks.

The presence of extra values in private keys (p, q, d mod (p-1), d mod (q-1), and the CRT coefficient) are intended for efficiency, as Quisquater and Couvreur demonstrated. These can be computed from the modulus and private exponent if needed.

Later analysis showed vulnerabilities in PKCS #1 v1.5 padding for encryption. Newer schemes like OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) are now preferred for encryption, while RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 remains acceptable for signatures when proper padding rules are followed.
sections.plainLanguage: Padding must be done right. If you do it sloppily, clever attackers can break the encryption.
